unit.title: Teaching programming and algorithms at university

video.title: Asymptotic analysis: Big-O, Θ and Ω
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Joseph - computer science lecturer, Nairobi
Dr Amina Bello - lecturer in education, Lagos
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: A student's search runs in a blink on ten thousand records. On the university's ten million, it never finishes. Their code was correct. What did they miss?
Today: what Big-O really says, why students confuse it with speed, and how to teach growth rates so they stick.
Big-O describes how running time grows as the input grows. It ignores constant factors and small inputs. It is an upper bound, while Theta gives a tight bound and Omega a lower one.
We write f of n is O of g of n when some constant c and some n zero exist with f at most c times g for every n beyond n zero. The definition is about the eventual shape of the curve.

A loop inside a loop over n items does n squared steps. Halving the range each time, as binary search does, takes about log n steps. At ten million records, that is a hundred trillion steps against about twenty four.
Divide-and-conquer algorithms give recurrences such as T of n equals two T of n over two plus n. The master theorem solves the common forms. Merge sort comes out at n log n.

Students often think Big-O means seconds, or that O of n squared is always slower than O of n. Let them time two algorithms on growing inputs and plot the curves. Then introduce the definition to explain what they saw.
Quick check! One algorithm takes one hundred n steps, another takes n squared. For large n, which is slower?
The n squared one, once n passes one hundred. Below that, it is actually faster. Big-O tells you who wins in the end, not who wins on small inputs.
In the app, open the Big-O lab. Grow the input and watch the step counts of different algorithms pull apart.
Your turn. A student says linear search is O of n squared. Is that statement true?
True, but not tight: O is only an upper bound, and Theta of n is the precise answer. Remember: Big-O is about growth, constants vanish, and recurrences solve divide and conquer.

scenes.narration: Try it in your next lecture: give pairs insertion sort and merge sort, and inputs from ten to ten thousand. They time both and plot the results. Then ask which curve matches n log n.

checkpoints.prompt: One algorithm takes 100n steps, another n². For large n, which is slower?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: beyond n = 100, n² grows past 100n.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: constants don't change the eventual winner; n² overtakes 100n at n = 100.

checkpoints.prompt: A student says linear search is O(n²). Is that true?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: O is an upper bound; Θ(n) is the tight one.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: n ≤ n², so the bound holds; it just isn't tight.
